cantabri.t: The mountain people of northern Spain whose resistance in the Cantabrian Wars of 29 to 19 BCE brought Augustus himself to Iberia.
cantabri.o: The Cantabri lived in the Cantabrian mountains and coast of northern Spain, in modern Cantabria and parts of Burgos, Palencia and León, from about the 4th century BCE. They were a Celtic-speaking people organised in clans, living in hillforts.
cantabri.r: Their mountain economy was based on herding goats and cattle, acorn bread and limited farming, and Strabo noted customs in which daughters inherited and husbands brought dowries. Their warriors raided the plains and served as mercenaries; their cavalry manoeuvre, the Cantabrian circle, was adopted by the Romans. They were never united under a single ruler.
cantabri.e: Augustus opened the Cantabrian Wars in 29 BCE, campaigning in person in 26 BCE, but conquest was completed only by Agrippa in 19 BCE, after mass deportations. The land became part of Hispania Tarraconensis; the name later reappeared in the Duchy of Cantabria.

county-of-montbeliard.t: A French-speaking Lutheran enclave ruled by the dukes of Württemberg for four centuries before France annexed it in 1793.
county-of-montbeliard.o: Montbéliard guarded the Belfort Gap between the Jura and the Vosges. Around 1042 Louis of Mousson, who also held Bar through his wife Sophie, ruled it as count. Later houses of Montfaucon and Chalon held it, all within the Kingdom of Arles and so in the Holy Roman Empire.
county-of-montbeliard.r: In 1397 the heiress Henriette of Montbéliard was betrothed to Eberhard IV of Württemberg, and the county passed to the Württemberg dynasty. From the 1520s, after preaching by Guillaume Farel, it became Lutheran, an unusual Protestant enclave between Catholic Franche-Comté and Alsace. Duke Frederick I ruled it from 1581 and brought in the architect Heinrich Schickhardt.
county-of-montbeliard.e: French troops occupied the county several times, and in 1793 the French First Republic annexed it. Württemberg recognised the loss in 1796. The region kept its Lutheran heritage and later became the home of the Peugeot industrial dynasty.

cerretani.t: The Pyrenean people of Cerdanya, famed in Roman times for their hams, whose name lives on in the Cerdanya valley.
cerretani.o: The Cerretani occupied the high Pyrenean valley of Cerdanya and the upper Segre, today divided between Spain, France and Andorra. They probably spoke an Iberian language, and are recorded from the late Iron Age.
cerretani.r: They lived from pastoralism and farming in the mountains, and Strabo noted that their hams were highly prized and profitable. Little is known of their political organisation. Their valley controlled routes across the Pyrenees between the Ebro basin and Gaul.
cerretani.e: They came under Roman control in the 2nd century BCE as part of Hispania Citerior. Pliny the Elder names the Roman town of Iulia Libica, modern Llívia, in their territory, and the name of the people survives in the region of Cerdanya.

county-of-foix.t: A Pyrenean county that sheltered Cathars, produced the hunter-prince Gaston Fébus and passed through Navarre to Henry IV.
county-of-foix.o: Around 1012 the lands of the count of Carcassonne were divided, and his son Bernard-Roger received the region around Foix, which became a separate county under the castle above the Ariège. His son Roger I is the first to be called count of Foix.
county-of-foix.r: The counts ruled a mountainous land of pasture and iron mines. Count Raymond-Roger fought the crusaders in the Albigensian Crusade, and many of his family supported the Cathars. In 1290 the counts inherited Béarn, and Gaston III Fébus ruled both from Orthez as a near-sovereign prince and wrote a famous hunting book.
county-of-foix.e: The house of Foix inherited the throne of Navarre in 1479, then passed to the Albrets. Through Jeanne d'Albret it reached Henry IV, who in 1607 united his personal lands, including Foix, with the Kingdom of France.

county-of-savoy.t: The Alpine county that controlled the Mont Cenis and Great St Bernard passes, the cradle of the house of Savoy and of later Italian kings.
county-of-savoy.o: Humbert White-Hands, a noble of the Kingdom of Arles, held counties around Maurienne and Savoy from around 1003. His son Odo married Adelaide of Turin, bringing lands in Piedmont, so the dynasty straddled the Alps from its beginnings.
county-of-savoy.r: The counts drew their power from controlling the main passes between France and Italy and from tolls on the trade that crossed them. Peter II, called the 'little Charlemagne', won the Vaud in the 13th century, and Chambéry became the capital in 1295. Amadeus VI, the Green Count, led a crusade in 1366, and Amadeus VII acquired Nice in 1388.
county-of-savoy.e: In 1416 Emperor Sigismund raised Amadeus VIII to the rank of duke, and the county became the Duchy of Savoy. The dynasty went on to rule Sardinia and, from 1861, all Italy.

contestani.t: The Iberian people of Alicante and Murcia whose sculptors produced the Lady of Elche, the masterpiece of Iberian art.
contestani.o: The Contestani occupied the coast and hinterland of south-east Spain, roughly the modern provinces of Alicante and parts of Murcia and Valencia, from the 5th century BCE. They grew out of earlier Iberian communities in close contact with Phoenician and Greek traders.
contestani.r: Their towns, such as Ilici (La Alcudia, Elche), La Serreta near Alcoy and Lucentum, were centres of a refined Iberian culture. The stone bust of the Lady of Elche, carved around the 4th century BCE, comes from their territory. They wrote their Iberian language in a Greek-derived alphabet, recorded on lead tablets, and traded olive oil, wine and esparto.
contestani.e: After Carthaginian control under Barcid Iberia, the region passed to Rome when Scipio captured Carthago Nova in 209 BCE, and was pacified by 197 BCE. Ilici became a Roman colony, and the Contestani merged into Hispania Citerior.

cauci.t: People of Ireland's east coast recorded only in Ptolemy's 2nd-century Geography, whose name echoes the Chauci of northern Germany.
cauci.o: The Cauci are known solely from Ptolemy's Geography of about 150, which drew on earlier reports by merchants and sailors. He places them on the east coast of Ireland, between the Eblani to the north and the Manapii to the south, roughly in the area of modern Dublin and Wicklow.
cauci.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers, settlements or way of life. Their name closely resembles that of the Chauci, a Germanic people of the North Sea coast, which has prompted speculation about settlers or traders from the Continent, but most scholars treat the likeness as coincidence or a copying error.
cauci.e: No later source mentions them, and Irish tradition preserves no matching name. Their region later formed part of the Kingdom of Leinster.

cassi.t: British people named only by Julius Caesar in 54 BCE, sometimes linked by name with Cassivellaunus, leader of resistance to Rome.
cassi.o: The Cassi are recorded once in Caesar's Gallic War as one of five British peoples, with the Cenimagni, Segontiaci, Ancalites and Bibroci, who sent envoys to surrender during his second invasion in 54 BCE.
cassi.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or society. Because their name resembles that of Cassivellaunus, some historians suggest they were his own people or a group within his following north of the Thames, perhaps in Hertfordshire, but there is no firm evidence.
cassi.e: They do not appear again in any source. Their territory, wherever it lay, was absorbed into larger polities such as the Catuvellauni before the Roman conquest of 43.

cornavii-caithness.t: People of Caithness at the northern tip of mainland Britain, recorded by Ptolemy and named after their headlands.
cornavii-caithness.o: Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 places the Cornavii in the far north-east of mainland Scotland, in modern Caithness. Their name, from a Celtic word for horn, probably means 'people of the promontory', referring to headlands such as Duncansby Head or Dunnet Head; the same name was borne by the Cornovii of the English Midlands and by the people of Cornwall.
cornavii-caithness.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers. Caithness has one of the densest concentrations of brochs in Scotland, tall drystone towers built in the last centuries BCE, which point to a society of powerful local families controlling fertile farmland and coastal resources.
cornavii-caithness.e: The Cornavii do not appear after Ptolemy. Caithness later formed part of the lands of the northern Picts before falling under Norse rule as part of the earldom of Orkney in the 9th and 10th centuries.

cumae.t: The oldest Greek colony on the Italian mainland, home of the Sibyl, which passed the Greek alphabet to the Etruscans and Latins.
cumae.o: Euboean Greeks from Chalcis and Eretria founded Cumae around 740 BCE on the Campanian coast north of the Bay of Naples, having first settled the island of Pithekoussai (Ischia). The site, a steep acropolis above the sea, controlled the fertile Phlegraean Fields and gave access to Etruscan and native trade.
cumae.r: Cumae was an aristocratic city that became a major power in the Tyrrhenian world. Its version of the Greek alphabet was adopted by the Etruscans and, through them, by Rome. The cave of the Sibyl and the temple of Apollo made it a famous oracle. The tyrant Aristodemus defeated the Etruscans at Aricia around 504 BCE, and in 474 BCE Cumae and Hieron I of Syracuse destroyed an Etruscan fleet off the city. Cumae also founded Neapolis.
cumae.e: Around 421 BCE Samnite-speaking Campanians captured Cumae, and it became an Oscan town. It received Roman citizenship without the vote in 338 BCE, later became a Roman municipium and declined as nearby Puteoli grew. A Byzantine fortress in the 6th century CE, it was finally destroyed by Naples in 1207.

commune-of-milan.t: The leading city-republic of Lombardy, razed by Frederick Barbarossa in 1162 and then at the head of the league that defeated him at Legnano.
commune-of-milan.o: Milan's archbishops had long dominated the city, but by 1097 consuls drawn from nobles and citizens were governing it. The young commune extended its power over the surrounding countryside and over neighbours such as Lodi and Como, whose complaints drew Emperor Frederick Barbarossa into Italy.
commune-of-milan.r: Government passed from consuls to a podestà, usually an outsider, alongside councils and the popular credenza di Sant'Ambrogio. Milan was a manufacturing centre for wool cloth and arms, with its own Ambrosian liturgy. Barbarossa destroyed the city in 1162, but it was rebuilt, joined the Lombard League and helped defeat the emperor at Legnano in 1176, winning self-government at the Peace of Constance in 1183.
commune-of-milan.e: Rivalry between nobles and the popular party opened the way to strongmen. In 1259 Martino della Torre was made lord of the people, and the commune gave way to the Lordship of Milan, later dominated by the Visconti.

croton.t: Achaean Greek city of southern Italy famed for its athletes, its doctors and Pythagoras, which destroyed Sybaris in 510 BCE.
croton.o: Achaean colonists led by Myscellus of Rhypes founded Croton around 710 BCE on the Ionian coast of Calabria, reportedly on the advice of the Delphic oracle. It had a good harbour and a broad territory, and became one of the major powers of Magna Graecia.
croton.r: Croton produced more Olympic victors than any other city in some periods, above all the wrestler Milo. It was renowned for medicine, with Democedes and Alcmaeon. Around 530 BCE Pythagoras settled there, and his followers dominated politics for a time before being violently overthrown. The sanctuary of Hera Lacinia at Capo Colonna was a religious centre for the Italiote Greeks. After defeat by Locri at the Sagras river, Croton crushed Sybaris in 510 BCE.
croton.e: In the 4th century Croton suffered from Dionysius I, who held it from 379 BCE, and from the Bruttians and Agathocles. During the war with Pyrrhus it was taken by Rome in 277 BCE. A Roman colony was founded there in 194 BCE, and the town survives as Crotone.

capua.t: The great city of Campania, Etruscan in origin and later Oscan, whose defection to Hannibal in 216 BCE ended in harsh Roman punishment.
capua.o: Capua lay in the fertile Campanian plain near the Volturno, on the site of modern Santa Maria Capua Vetere. The Etruscans developed it into a city in the 7th and 6th centuries BCE as the centre of their Campanian holdings. Around 423 BCE Oscan-speaking Samnites seized it, and its people became known as Campani.
capua.r: Capua grew rich on grain, wine, bronze-working and perfumes, and Romans saw it as a centre of luxury. It was governed by a chief magistrate, the meddix tuticus, and a senate. Threatened by the Samnites, it appealed to Rome in 343 BCE, triggering the First Samnite War, and from 338 BCE its citizens held Roman citizenship without the vote. Its Mother Goddess sanctuary yielded hundreds of stone statues of women with infants.
capua.e: After Cannae in 216 BCE Capua went over to Hannibal. Rome besieged it and took it in 211 BCE, executed its leaders, confiscated its land and abolished its self-government. It recovered as a Roman colony and later saw the slave revolt of Spartacus begin in its gladiator school in 73 BCE.

county-of-sicily.t: The Norman county that conquered Muslim Sicily and built the multilingual, multi-faith government later inherited by the Kingdom of Sicily.
county-of-sicily.o: Roger de Hauteville, Robert Guiscard's youngest brother, crossed to Sicily in 1061 and took Messina. With Guiscard he besieged Palermo, which fell in early 1072, and Roger became count of Sicily under his brother's overlordship. The conquest of the Emirate of Sicily took thirty years, ending with the fall of Noto in 1091, the year Roger also raided Malta.
county-of-sicily.r: Roger ruled a largely Muslim and Greek population with a thin Norman elite. He kept Arabic-speaking fiscal offices, recruited Muslim troops, refounded Latin bishoprics and endowed Greek monasteries. In 1098 Pope Urban II granted him unusual control over the Sicilian church. After his death in 1101, his widow Adelaide del Vasto ruled as regent and moved the court to Palermo.
county-of-sicily.e: Roger II came of age in 1112, absorbed the mainland Duchy of Apulia and Calabria in 1127 and was crowned king at Palermo on Christmas Day 1130. The county thus became the core of the Kingdom of Sicily.
county-of-sicily.re: Catholic Christianity, with Greek Orthodox Christianity and Sunni Islam
county-of-sicily.la: Arabic, Greek, Latin, Old Norman French

cessetani.t: The Iberian people of the Tarragona area, near whose town Kese the Romans won their first battle in Iberia in 218 BCE.
cessetani.o: The Cessetani, or Cosetani, inhabited the Camp de Tarragona and the lower Penedès in southern Catalonia from about the 5th century BCE. Their main settlement was Kese, usually located at or near Tarragona.
cessetani.r: Their territory had fortified settlements such as Alorda Park at Calafell and lived from farming and trade along the coast. Kese minted widely circulated coins with an Iberian legend. Their political structure is not recorded, but they were prosperous enough for both Carthage and Rome to value the area.
cessetani.e: In 218 BCE Gnaeus Scipio defeated the Carthaginian commander Hanno near Cissa, and the Romans established their base at Tarraco. The region thus became Rome's first foothold in Iberia, and Tarraco grew into the capital of Hispania Citerior and later Tarraconensis.

county-of-luxembourg.t: The castle-county on the Alzette that gave the Holy Roman Empire four emperors and grew into the duchy behind today's Grand Duchy.
county-of-luxembourg.o: In 963 Count Siegfried acquired the rock of Lucilinburhuc from the abbey of St Maximin at Trier and built a castle there. His descendants, and from 1136 the counts of Namur and later Limburg lines, expanded the county through the Ardennes and Moselle valley.
county-of-luxembourg.r: Luxembourg was a bilingual land of German and French speakers. Count Henry VII became emperor in 1308, and his son John the Blind, king of Bohemia, died at Crécy in 1346. Emperor Charles IV raised the county to a duchy in 1354. The fortress city became one of Europe's strongest, later rebuilt by Vauban.
county-of-luxembourg.e: Elisabeth of Görlitz ceded the duchy to Philip the Good of the Burgundian State in 1443. It then passed with the Habsburg Netherlands to the Spanish Netherlands and Austrian Netherlands, was briefly French in 1684–1697, and was annexed by France in 1795. It was revived as the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg in 1815.

commune-of-brescia.t: A combative Lombard city-republic, home of the reformer Arnold of Brescia, that withstood a siege by Emperor Frederick II in 1238.
commune-of-brescia.o: Brescia's citizens took power from their bishop in the late 11th and early 12th centuries, and the commune was governed by consuls by around 1100. It controlled a rich territory of valleys, iron mines and lakes between Lake Garda and Lake Iseo.
commune-of-brescia.r: The commune was run by consuls and later a podestà. The preacher Arnold of Brescia, who attacked clerical wealth, came from the city. Brescia joined the Lombard League against Frederick Barbarossa, resisted a long siege by Frederick II in 1238 and another by Henry VII in 1311. It was famed for iron working and arms making, and its Old Cathedral, the Rotonda, dates from this era.
commune-of-brescia.e: Exhausted by faction, Brescia accepted the Scaliger lords of Verona and then in 1337 submitted to Azzone Visconti, joining the Lordship of Milan. The Republic of Venice took it in 1426.

county-palatine-of-chester.t: A Norman marcher earldom on the Welsh border whose earls ruled Cheshire almost as independent princes.
county-palatine-of-chester.o: After crushing northern and Mercian resistance, William the Conqueror gave the earldom of Chester to Gerbod the Fleming and then, in 1071, to Hugh d'Avranches. Its purpose was to guard the northern Welsh border and push into Gwynedd.
county-palatine-of-chester.r: The earls held nearly all of Cheshire, with their own courts, sheriff and barons, and royal writs did not normally run there, a status later called palatine. Hugh and his cousin Robert of Rhuddlan advanced along the north Welsh coast. Ranulf de Gernon and Ranulf de Blondeville were major figures in the wars of Stephen and John; Ranulf III built Beeston Castle.
county-palatine-of-chester.e: When John the Scot, the last earl of the line, died childless in 1237, Henry III took the earldom into royal hands. From 1301 it was given to the heir to the throne, and Cheshire kept palatine institutions until 1830.

county-of-blois.t: The Loire county of the Thibaudian counts, rivals of the early Capetians, whose family gave England King Stephen and later united with Champagne.
county-of-blois.o: Theobald the Trickster, a vassal of Hugh the Great, held Blois, Chartres and Tours by around 940 and founded a dynasty. His grandson Odo II added Troyes and Meaux around 1022, encircling the Capetian royal domain and contending with Anjou for Touraine, which was lost in 1044.
county-of-blois.r: The counts ruled a rich farming land of the Loire and the Beauce, with Chartres and its cathedral school a major centre of learning. Count Stephen-Henry, husband of Adela of Normandy, was a leader of the First Crusade, and their son Stephen became king of England in 1135. The family's Champagne branch, ruling the County of Champagne, became the more powerful line.
county-of-blois.e: From the 1230s the house of Châtillon held Blois. The last count, Guy II, sold it to Louis of Orléans in 1391, with possession at his death in 1397. When Louis's grandson, born at Blois, became Louis XII in 1498, it joined the Kingdom of France.

carpetani.t: A people of the central Meseta around Toledo and Madrid, defeated by Hannibal on the Tagus before Rome absorbed their lands.
carpetani.o: The Carpetani occupied the upper and middle Tagus basin, in modern Madrid, Toledo and Ciudad Real, from the second half of the first millennium BCE. Their language is thought to have been Celtic, though Iberian influences were strong.
carpetani.r: They lived in fortified towns such as Toletum and Complutum, on a farming and herding economy of the open plateau. Their political organisation is little known, but they could field large armies. In 220 BCE Hannibal defeated a coalition of Carpetani, Olcades and Vaccaei at the crossing of the Tagus.
carpetani.e: Rome reached their land in the early 2nd century BCE: Marcus Fulvius Nobilior took Toletum in 193 BCE, and Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus pacified the region by 179 BCE. They became part of Hispania Citerior, and Toletum grew into Roman and later Visigothic Toledo.

county-of-vermandois.t: A Picard county held by descendants of Charlemagne, whose counts were king-makers in 10th-century France before the land returned to the crown.
county-of-vermandois.o: Herbert I, a Carolingian descended from Bernard of Italy, became count of Vermandois around 896, with his seat at Saint-Quentin. His family built up lands across Picardy and Champagne during the struggles between the Carolingian kings and the Robertians.
county-of-vermandois.r: Herbert II was the most powerful lord of northern France in the 920s, holding King Charles the Simple prisoner at Péronne until the king's death in 929 and seizing the archbishopric of Reims for his young son. Later counts were less prominent. Around 1080 the heiress Adelaide married Hugh of Vermandois, brother of King Philip I and a leader of the First Crusade.
county-of-vermandois.e: In the 12th century the county passed by marriage to Philip of Alsace, count of Flanders, who lost much of it to Philip II of France in the Treaty of Boves in 1185. After the death of Countess Eleanor in 1213 the rest was absorbed by the Kingdom of France.

chios.t: Rich Ionian island state, famed for its wine and mastic, a major naval power and home of the Homeridae who claimed descent from Homer.
chios.o: Ionian Greeks settled Chios, a large island off the Erythrae peninsula, c. 1000 BCE, and it became one of the twelve members of the Ionian League. By the 7th century BCE it was a wealthy trading state with an early written law code, suggesting a council with popular elements.
chios.r: Chios exported wine and mastic and was said to be the first Greek state to buy slaves. The Homeridae guild of poets claimed descent from Homer. It sent 100 ships to the Battle of Lade in 494 BCE. In the Delian League it kept its own fleet, before revolting in 412 BCE and later leaving the Second Athenian League in the Social War of 357 BCE.
chios.e: In 86 BCE Mithridates of the Kingdom of Pontus deported the Chians to the Black Sea; Sulla restored them and Rome confirmed their freedom. The island stayed prosperous under Roman rule and later Genoese and Ottoman masters.

county-palatine-of-cephalonia-and-zakynt.t: Ionian island county ruled by the Orsini and Tocco families for three centuries, a link between Italy, the Frankish Morea and Epirus.
county-palatine-of-cephalonia-and-zakynt.o: In 1185 the Norman admiral Margaritus of Brindisi took Cephalonia and Zakynthos from Byzantium for William II of Sicily. By about 1195 the islands were held by Matthew Orsini, of an Apulian family, who founded a hereditary lordship and placed himself in turn under the protection of the Pope, Venice and the Principality of Achaea.
county-palatine-of-cephalonia-and-zakynt.r: The counts ruled a Greek Orthodox population through Italian and Greek officials, with a Latin bishop alongside the Orthodox clergy. The Orsini intermarried with the rulers of the Despotate of Epirus and later acquired it. In 1357 the county passed to Leonardo I Tocco, and his son Carlo I Tocco extended Tocco power to Ioannina and Arta.
county-palatine-of-cephalonia-and-zakynt.e: Leonardo III Tocco lost his mainland lands to the Ottomans and in 1479 the islands as well, fleeing to Italy. Venice won Zakynthos in 1485 and Cephalonia in 1500, making them part of the Venetian Ionian Islands.

cyme-aeolis.t: The largest of the Aeolian cities on the Anatolian coast, home of Hesiod's father and the historian Ephorus.
cyme-aeolis.o: Aeolian Greeks founded Cyme on the coast north of the Hermus, near modern Aliağa, c. 1000 BCE. It became the leading city of the Aeolian dodecapolis, and tradition held that Hesiod's father sailed from Cyme to Boeotia. A Cymaean princess was said to have married King Midas of Phrygia.
cyme-aeolis.r: Cyme was a commercial port, minting coins from the 6th century BCE. It fell to the Kingdom of Lydia and then the Achaemenid Empire; its tyrant Aristagoras was among those guarding Darius's bridge over the Danube c. 513 BCE. The city joined the Ionian Revolt and later the Delian League, and the historian Ephorus was born there in the 4th century BCE.
cyme-aeolis.e: In the Hellenistic period Cyme passed between Seleucid and Pergamene control and kept its civic institutions. It came under Rome when the province of Asia was organised in 129 BCE, and remained a modest city into late antiquity.

cynetes.t: The people of the Algarve, named by Herodotus as the westernmost inhabitants of Europe and linked to the enigmatic south-western script.
cynetes.o: The Cynetes, or Conii, lived in the far south of modern Portugal, in the Algarve and lower Alentejo. Herodotus in the 5th century BCE called them the most westerly people of Europe, beyond the Celts. Their lands lay on the Atlantic routes that connected Tartessos with the north.
cynetes.r: Their region holds most of the inscribed stone stelae in the south-western script, the oldest writing in Iberia, dated to the 7th to 5th centuries BCE; the language they record is undeciphered and debated. Little is known of their political organisation, though Appian names a town, Conistorgis, as their chief place.
cynetes.e: In 153 BCE Lusitanians raiding Roman territory captured Conistorgis, then held by allies of Rome. The Cynetes were absorbed into the Roman province of Hispania Ulterior and later Lusitania, and their name disappears from the record.

catuvellauni.t: The leading power of late Iron Age Britain, whose king Cunobelinus ruled much of the south-east and whose sons led resistance to the Roman invasion of 43.
catuvellauni.o: The Catuvellauni held the lands north of the Thames around Hertfordshire. Cassivellaunus, who commanded British resistance to Julius Caesar in 54 BCE, is usually thought to have been their leader, with his stronghold perhaps at Wheathampstead. By the late 1st century BCE their king Tasciovanus was minting coins at Verlamion, near modern St Albans.
catuvellauni.r: Their rulers issued abundant gold coinage, some styled with the Latin REX, and imported wine, silver and fine pottery from the Roman world, as rich burials at Welwyn and Folly Lane show. Cunobelinus, ruling from about 9 to 40 CE from Camulodunum, which he took from the Trinovantes, extended influence over Kent and much of the south-east; Suetonius called him king of the Britons.
catuvellauni.e: After Cunobelinus died, his sons Togodumnus and Caratacus provoked Rome by attacking the Atrebates (Britain). Claudius invaded in 43; Togodumnus was killed and Caratacus fled west to fight on among the Silures and Ordovices until 51. The tribe became the civitas Catuvellaunorum, centred on Verulamium, in Roman Britain.

corinth.t: Wealthy trading city on the Isthmus, founder of Syracuse and Corcyra and a leading power of Archaic Greece, destroyed by Rome in 146 BCE.
corinth.o: Corinth grew in the early Iron Age on the Isthmus linking the Peloponnese to central Greece, below the fortress hill of Acrocorinth. Dorian settlers formed the city, and from the 8th century BCE it was governed by the Bacchiad clan, who founded Corcyra and Syracuse in 733 BCE.
corinth.r: Cypselus overthrew the Bacchiads c. 657 BCE, and his son Periander made Corinth a major power. Corinthian pottery dominated Mediterranean markets in the 7th century BCE, and the diolkos let ships be dragged across the Isthmus. After the tyranny an oligarchy ruled, and Corinth was a key ally in the Peloponnesian League; its quarrels with Corcyra and Athens helped start the Peloponnesian War.
corinth.e: Corinth fought Sparta in the Corinthian War of 395 to 387 BCE. Macedonian kings garrisoned Acrocorinth until Aratus took it for the Achaean League in 243 BCE. Lucius Mummius destroyed Corinth in 146 BCE; Julius Caesar refounded it as a Roman colony in 44 BCE.
corinth.re: Greek religion; cults of Poseidon and Aphrodite

county-of-ponthieu.t: A small county at the mouth of the Somme where Harold Godwinson was held captive and where the English won at Crécy.
county-of-ponthieu.o: Ponthieu emerged around 980 when Hugh, a castellan of Abbeville, married a daughter of Hugh Capet and was recognised as count. Abbeville became the seat of a modest dynasty on the coast between Normandy and Flanders.
county-of-ponthieu.r: The counts profited from the Somme estuary and the cloth and salt trades. In 1064 Count Guy I captured the shipwrecked Harold Godwinson and handed him to William of Normandy, as shown on the Bayeux Tapestry. In 1279 the county passed through Eleanor of Castile to her husband Edward I of England.
county-of-ponthieu.e: The English kings held Ponthieu as vassals of France; Edward III fought at Crécy, inside the county, in 1346, and the Treaty of Brétigny of 1360 gave it to him in full sovereignty. French forces reconquered it in 1369, and it joined the Kingdom of France, later passing briefly to Burgundy.

caledonii.t: Confederation of the Scottish Highlands that fought Agricola at Mons Graupius and Septimius Severus, and gave its name to Caledonia.
caledonii.o: The Caledonii were a people of the central and northern Highlands, named by Ptolemy and others; Roman writers used Caledonia for northern Britain as a whole. They first appear in history when the governor Agricola marched north, and Tacitus says a host of Caledonian peoples gathered under Calgacus to meet him at Mons Graupius in 83 or 84.
caledonii.r: Romans describe them as a warrior society of clans and chiefs, without towns or coinage, living by herding and farming in a landscape of roundhouses, crannogs and brochs further north. Cassius Dio later portrays the Caledonians and Maeatae as the two main groupings beyond the walls, and tells of the Caledonian Argentocoxus, whose wife bantered with the empress Julia Domna.
caledonii.e: Defeated at Mons Graupius but never conquered, the Caledonians bought peace or raided as Roman power allowed. Septimius Severus campaigned against them from 208 to 211, and after his death Rome withdrew. By the late 3rd century Roman writers spoke instead of the Picts, whose Kingdom of the Picts absorbed the Caledonian peoples.

celtiberians.t: Celtic-speaking peoples of the central Iberian plateau whose long resistance to Rome ended with the fall of Numantia in 133 BCE.
celtiberians.o: The Celtiberians took shape from about the 6th century BCE in the upper Ebro, Douro and Tagus basins, in modern Soria, Guadalajara, Zaragoza and Cuenca. Ancient writers saw them as a mix of Celts and Iberians; they spoke a Celtic language and included peoples such as the Arevaci, Belli, Titti and Lusones.
celtiberians.r: They lived in fortified hill towns, or oppida, governed by councils and assemblies, with strong warrior elites, client bonds and hospitality pacts recorded on bronze tablets. They wrote Celtiberian in an adapted Iberian script, as on the Botorrita bronzes, and were famed for their swords, later adopted by the Roman army as the gladius hispaniensis.
celtiberians.e: Rome fought the Celtiberian Wars from 181 to 133 BCE, ending with Scipio Aemilianus' siege and destruction of Numantia. Many later backed Sertorius, and after his death in 72 BCE they were absorbed into Hispania Citerior and Romanised.

county-of-la-marche.t: A border county between Poitou and the Limousin, held by the Lusignans at the height of their power and later by Armagnac and Bourbon princes.
county-of-la-marche.o: La Marche took its name from its position as a frontier zone, or march, of the duchy of Aquitaine. Around 958 Boso the Old, a lord of Charroux, held comital authority there, and his descendants ruled both La Marche and the neighbouring Périgord.
county-of-la-marche.r: A poor upland county of pasture and woodland, La Marche mattered for its strategic place between the Plantagenet and Capetian spheres. From 1199 the Lusignans held it; Hugh X married Isabella of Angoulême, widow of King John, and joined a failed revolt against Louis IX in 1242. Guéret and Charroux were its main centres.
county-of-la-marche.e: After the Lusignan line ended in 1308, Philip IV took the county. It passed to the Bourbons, the Armagnacs and back to the Bourbons as an appanage, until Francis I confiscated the lands of Constable Charles of Bourbon in 1523. It was united with the Kingdom of France in 1527.

commune-of-asti.t: A Piedmontese city-republic whose merchants and money-lenders spread across France and Flanders, giving the 'Lombard' bankers their name in the north.
commune-of-asti.o: Asti had long been ruled by its bishops, but consuls representing the citizens are recorded in 1095, making it one of the earliest communes in Piedmont. It grew rich on the trade route between Lombardy, the Alpine passes and France, and resisted both its bishop and the March of Montferrat.
commune-of-asti.r: The commune was run by consuls and later a podestà, with powerful merchant families building tower houses in the city. Asti's financiers set up pawn and loan banks across France, Savoy, the Low Countries and the Rhineland. Frederick Barbarossa burned the city in 1155, but it recovered and won a wide rural territory. The Palio of Asti horse race is first recorded in 1275.
commune-of-asti.e: Faction strife between the Solaro and de Castello families led the city to submit to outside lords, including the Angevins, and in 1342 to Luchino Visconti of the Lordship of Milan. Asti later passed as a dowry to the Orléans and then to the Duchy of Savoy.

commune-of-pavia.t: The old Lombard royal capital turned city-republic, a loyal imperial ally and Milan's bitter rival until the Visconti took it in 1359.
commune-of-pavia.o: Pavia had been the capital of the Kingdom of the Lombards and the coronation city of the Kingdom of Italy (medieval). Around 1100 its citizens organised a commune under consuls, inheriting the city's royal palace traditions and a renowned school of law.
commune-of-pavia.r: Consuls and later a podestà ruled the city, which stood firmly with the emperors against Milan, fighting it repeatedly in the 12th and 13th centuries. Pavia controlled the confluence of the Ticino and the Po and much of the Lomellina. Its churches, such as San Michele Maggiore where kings were crowned and San Pietro in Ciel d'Oro with Saint Augustine's tomb, reflected its royal past. The Beccaria family dominated in the 14th century.
commune-of-pavia.e: Galeazzo II Visconti captured Pavia in 1359 after a long siege, absorbing it into the Lordship of Milan. The Visconti built a castle there, founded the university in 1361 and later the Certosa di Pavia.

county-of-boulogne.t: A Channel-coast county whose counts fought at Hastings, ruled Crusader Jerusalem and married into the English throne.
county-of-boulogne.o: Boulogne took shape in the late 9th and early 10th centuries under counts linked to the house of Flanders; Adalulf, a son of Baldwin II of Flanders, held it in the 910s. The port's position on the shortest crossing to England shaped its history from the start.
county-of-boulogne.r: The counts drew wealth from the port, cross-Channel trade and lands in England. Eustace II fought for William the Conqueror at Hastings in 1066, and his sons Godfrey of Bouillon and Baldwin I led the First Crusade and ruled Jerusalem. Countess Matilda married Stephen of England. Count Renaud de Dammartin fought against Philip II at Bouvines in 1214 and lost his lands.
county-of-boulogne.e: The county passed through the houses of Auvergne and La Tour before the Burgundian State took it in 1435. After Charles the Bold's death, Louis XI seized it in 1477 and placed it under the Virgin of Boulogne, holding it directly for the Kingdom of France.

caereni.t: People of the far north-west of Scotland, named only by Ptolemy, living on the Atlantic coast of Sutherland.
caereni.o: The Caereni appear in Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 on the north-western mainland of Scotland, north of the Carnonacae, usually located in western Sutherland around Assynt and Kinlochbervie. Their name has been interpreted as meaning 'sheep folk', though this is uncertain.
caereni.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers or institutions. The Atlantic coast of Sutherland was a thinly peopled land of rock, bog and sea lochs, and its inhabitants lived in roundhouses and brochs, herding livestock, fishing and farming small patches of better land.
caereni.e: The Caereni are not mentioned again. Their region later formed part of the lands of the Picts and from the 9th century came under the control of Norse settlers and the earls of Orkney.

county-of-aversa.t: The first Norman lordship in southern Italy, granted to mercenaries in 1030 and the springboard for the Norman conquest of the south.
county-of-aversa.o: In 1030 Duke Sergius IV of the Duchy of Naples rewarded the Norman mercenary leader Rainulf Drengot with the town and district of Aversa, between Naples and Capua, to guard his frontier against the Principality of Capua. Rainulf's band became a magnet for further adventurers arriving from Normandy.
county-of-aversa.r: Aversa was a military lordship in which a small warrior elite of French-speaking Normans ruled a Lombard and Italo-Romance population. Its counts sold their swords to whichever of Naples, Capua, Salerno or the Byzantines paid best, gaining recognition from Emperor Conrad II in 1038. Rainulf founded a bishopric in the town, and the county drew in Norman knights who later served in Apulia.
county-of-aversa.e: In 1058 Count Richard Drengot captured Capua and took the title of prince. Aversa was absorbed into the Principality of Capua, and its warriors had by then helped launch the conquests that created the Duchy of Apulia and Calabria.

chalcidian-league.t: Federation of the Greek towns of Chalcidice centred on Olynthus, the strongest power of the northern Aegean until Philip II of Macedon destroyed it.
chalcidian-league.o: In 432 BCE the Chalcidian towns, persuaded by Perdiccas II of Macedon, revolted from the Delian League, and many of their people moved into Olynthus. From this union grew a federal state calling itself 'the Chalcidians'. With help from the Spartan Brasidas in 424 BCE it secured its independence from Athens.
chalcidian-league.r: Member towns shared citizenship, laws on marriage and property and a common silver coinage showing Apollo and his lyre, among the finest of the age. In the early 4th century BCE the league grew aggressively, absorbing Potidaea and even occupying Pella, the Macedonian capital, during the troubles of Amyntas III.
chalcidian-league.e: Appeals from Acanthus and Apollonia brought a Spartan war (382-379 BCE) that forced the league to dissolve. It revived, allied first with Philip II and then with Athens, but Philip besieged Olynthus and destroyed it in 348 BCE, ending the league and annexing Chalcidice to Macedon.

cait.t: A Pictish province in the far north of mainland Scotland, whose name survives in Caithness and in Gaelic Cataibh for Sutherland.
cait.o: Cait is one of the seven Pictish provinces named after the legendary sons of Cruithne. The name, perhaps 'cat people', survives in Caithness, the Norse 'headland of the Cats', and Gaelic Cataibh, the name for Sutherland.
cait.r: Nothing reliable is known of its government or rulers. Broch towers and later Pictish symbol stones show a long-settled farming and seafaring population in the region.
cait.e: From the 9th century Norse settlers from Orkney took over Caithness, which came under the Earldom of Orkney. The area was gradually brought into the Kingdom of Scotland in the 12th and 13th centuries.

cyprus-under-isaac-komnenos.t: Breakaway Byzantine realm on Cyprus ruled by the self-proclaimed emperor Isaac Komnenos until Richard the Lionheart conquered the island in 1191.
cyprus-under-isaac-komnenos.o: Isaac Komnenos, a great-nephew of Emperor Manuel I, had been governor in Cilicia and a prisoner of the Armenians. After his ransom he arrived in Cyprus in 1184 with forged imperial letters, took over the government and proclaimed himself emperor, refusing to recognise Andronikos I in Constantinople.
cyprus-under-isaac-komnenos.r: Isaac ruled from Nicosia with mercenaries and was remembered by Cypriots as harsh and grasping, seizing property and abusing local nobles. He secured his position by allying with William II of Sicily, whose fleet defeated a Byzantine expedition sent by Isaac II Angelos in 1186-1187, and reportedly with Saladin. The island remained Greek Orthodox and Greek-speaking.
cyprus-under-isaac-komnenos.e: In May 1191 ships of the Third Crusade carrying Richard I's sister and his betrothed Berengaria were stranded at Limassol. Isaac's mistreatment of them gave Richard a pretext: he conquered Cyprus within weeks and held Isaac in silver chains. Richard soon sold the island to the Knights Templar.

commune-of-ferrara.t: A Po delta city-republic whose factional wars ended with the Este family as perpetual lords, the start of one of Italy's great dynasties.
commune-of-ferrara.o: Ferrara was held by Matilda of Canossa, who besieged it in 1101 to put down a revolt. In the years that followed, citizens formed a commune under consuls, profiting from Po river traffic and salt. The cathedral was begun in 1135.
commune-of-ferrara.r: Consuls and later a podestà ruled, but power was really contested between noble factions: the Adelardi, the Ghibelline Torelli led by Salinguerra II Torelli, and the Guelph Este marquises. Ferrara's position on the Po made it a hub for trade between Venice and the Lombard plain. Azzo VII d'Este expelled Salinguerra in 1240 with Venetian and papal help.
commune-of-ferrara.e: After Azzo VII's death in 1264, the citizens proclaimed his grandson Obizzo II d'Este perpetual lord, and the commune gave way to the Duchy of Ferrara under the Este.

county-of-auvergne.t: The county of the volcanic Massif Central, centred on Clermont, where Pope Urban II preached the First Crusade in 1095.
county-of-auvergne.o: Auvergne was ruled in the late 9th century by William the Pious as part of his Aquitanian power. In the later 10th century the viscounts of Clermont took the comital title, and by around 980 they governed the county as hereditary counts under the loose overlordship of the dukes of Aquitaine.
county-of-auvergne.r: The county was a land of uplands, pasture and Romanesque churches, with the bishops of Clermont a rival power in the city. In 1095 Urban II proclaimed the First Crusade at the Council of Clermont. In the 12th century a family dispute split off the Dauphiné of Auvergne, and Philip II's campaigns from 1209 seized much of the county for the crown.
county-of-auvergne.e: The remaining county, centred on Vic-le-Comte, passed to the La Tour family and through Madeleine de la Tour d'Auvergne to her daughter Catherine de' Medici. The royal lands of Auvergne, held by the Bourbons, were confiscated after 1523 and united with the Kingdom of France in 1531.

county-palatine-of-durham.t: The palatinate where the bishops of Durham ruled as prince-bishops for more than seven centuries, guarding England's northern frontier.
county-palatine-of-durham.o: The bishops of Durham inherited the lands and prestige of the community of Saint Cuthbert, whose shrine moved to Durham in 995. William the Conqueror appointed Walcher of Lorraine bishop in 1071 and gave him the earldom of Northumbria in 1075, joining spiritual and secular power on the Scottish border.
county-palatine-of-durham.r: The bishops had their own courts, chancery, mint, sheriff and army, and royal writs did not normally run between the Tyne and the Tees. Durham Cathedral and Castle, built from 1093, expressed their power. Bishops such as Antony Bek and Thomas Langley were leading royal servants. Coal and lead mining added to their wealth.
county-palatine-of-durham.e: The Tudors curbed the palatinate's independence in 1536. The Durham (County Palatine) Act of 1836 transferred its remaining secular powers to the crown, and the University of Durham was founded with part of the bishops' endowment.

cenel-ngabrain.t: The dominant kindred of Dal Riata in Kintyre, whose kings, from Aedan mac Gabrain onwards, most often held the overkingship of Gaelic Argyll.
cenel-ngabrain.o: Cenel nGabrain traced its descent to Gabran, said to be a grandson of Fergus Mor, and held Kintyre, Arran and nearby lands in the 6th century. Its leading king, Aedan mac Gabrain, was ordained by Columba of Iona according to Adomnan, and campaigned widely in northern Britain before his defeat by Aethelfrith of Bernicia at Degsastan in 603.
cenel-ngabrain.r: The kindred controlled the hillfort of Dunadd for much of its history and competed with Cenel Loairn for the overkingship. Its rulers patronised Iona and fought both Picts and Britons of Alt Clut. The Senchus fer nAlban records its houses and duties to supply ships.
cenel-ngabrain.e: Defeat at Mag Rath in 637 under Domnall Brecc, and later Pictish conquest, eroded its standing. Kenneth MacAlpin, founder of the Kingdom of Scotland in the 840s, was traditionally counted among its descendants, giving the kindred a central place in Scottish royal genealogy.

county-of-forcalquier.t: A county of upper Provence that broke away from the main comital line and was reunited with Provence in 1209.
county-of-forcalquier.o: The county arose from the division of the inheritance of the counts of Provence in the mid-11th century, when one branch kept rights in the north-east around Forcalquier, Sisteron and the Durance valley. In the 12th century it passed to the counts of Urgell, who ruled it as a separate principality.
county-of-forcalquier.r: Forcalquier was a land of hill towns and pasture along the Durance, controlling routes between Provence and the Alps. Count William IV, the most prominent ruler, held out against the Catalan counts of Provence and the emperors for decades.
county-of-forcalquier.e: In 1193 William IV's granddaughter Garsenda married Alfonso II of Provence, and on William's death in 1209 Forcalquier was reunited with the County of Provence. Their son Raymond Berengar IV ruled both.

creones.t: People of the west Highland coast of Scotland, named only in Ptolemy's 2nd-century Geography.
creones.o: The Creones are known solely from Ptolemy's Geography of about 150, which places them on the western seaboard of Scotland north of the Epidii, usually located somewhere between Lorn, Ardnamurchan and Knoydart. Their name has no clear meaning, and some editors read it as a corrupted form.
creones.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers or society. The rugged coast and sea lochs of this region were settled in small communities living in duns, crannogs and roundhouses, relying on fishing, herding and limited farming. Ptolemy's information probably came from sailors who passed along the coast, perhaps during Agricola's fleet operations.
creones.e: The Creones are not mentioned again. Their region was later divided between the Gaelic kingdom of Dál Riata in the south and the Picts further north.

callaeci.t: The hillfort peoples of north-western Iberia, whose castro culture shaped Galicia and northern Portugal and who held out against Rome until 19 BCE.
callaeci.o: The Callaeci, or Gallaeci, occupied the north-west of Iberia north of the Douro, in modern Galicia and northern Portugal. Their culture grew from the Late Bronze Age into the Iron Age castro culture, marked by hundreds of fortified hilltop settlements of round stone houses.
callaeci.r: They were divided into many small communities rather than one state, each based on a castro such as Citânia de Briteiros or Santa Tecla. They mined gold and tin, worked bronze and gold into torcs, and built sauna-like bathhouses with carved stones. They spoke a Celtic language, worshipped gods such as Bandua, and erected stone warrior statues.
callaeci.e: Decimus Junius Brutus campaigned among them in 137 BCE and took the name Callaicus, but conquest was completed only in Augustus' Cantabrian Wars, ending in 19 BCE. Their land became the Roman region and later province of Gallaecia.

county-of-anjou.t: The Loire Valley county whose aggressive counts built the power base of the Plantagenets and later passed to a line of French royal princes.
county-of-anjou.o: Anjou emerged in the late 9th century, when the Frankish crown entrusted the region around Angers to local magnates facing Breton and Viking raids. Ingelger held authority there, and his son Fulk the Red was styled count by about 930, founding a dynasty that turned a frontier command into a hereditary principality.
county-of-anjou.r: The counts ruled from Angers with a dense network of stone castles, many built by Fulk Nerra (987–1040), which let them push into Touraine and Maine. Anjou was a wine and river-trade region with powerful abbeys. Geoffrey Plantagenet conquered Normandy in the 1140s, and his son Henry II joined Anjou to England and Aquitaine in the Angevin Empire.
county-of-anjou.e: Philip II of France seized Anjou in 1204. It was granted as an appanage to Charles of Anjou in 1246, became a duchy in 1360 for Louis I, and its last great duke, René of Anjou, died in 1480. Louis XI then annexed it to the Kingdom of France.

caristii.t: A small people of Bizkaia and Álava between the Deba and Nervión rivers, whose Roman town Veleia lay on the road to Gaul.
caristii.o: The Caristii lived in the later Iron Age between the Deba and Nervión rivers, in modern Bizkaia and northern Álava, flanked by the Autrigones and Varduli. Their language is unknown.
caristii.r: Their society of hillfort communities is little documented. Ptolemy names their towns as Suessatium, Tullonium and Veleia, the last of which grew into the Roman town of Iruña-Veleia.
caristii.e: They came under Roman control as the conquest of the north was completed in 19 BCE and were absorbed into Hispania Tarraconensis.

county-of-loon.t: A Limburg county around Borgloon and Hasselt that remained independent for three centuries before being absorbed by the prince-bishops of Liège.
county-of-loon.o: Counts of Loon appear around 1015, when Giselbert held lands around Borgloon in the Hesbaye. They expanded north into the Kempen heathlands, and the county became one of the middle-ranking principalities of Lower Lorraine.
county-of-loon.r: Loon was largely rural, with small towns such as Hasselt, Tongeren nearby and Borgloon. From the late 12th century the counts were vassals of the prince-bishops of Liège. The poet Henric van Veldeke, a founder of literature in Dutch and German, came from the county and wrote for its court circles.
county-of-loon.e: After Count Louis IV died childless in 1336, his inheritance was disputed between his heirs and the bishops of Liège. In 1366 the Prince-Bishopric of Liège annexed the county, and it remained part of the principality until 1795; it corresponds roughly to Belgian Limburg.

cortona.t: Etruscan hill city above the Val di Chiana, known for its monumental tumuli and the Tabula Cortonensis, one of the longest Etruscan texts.
cortona.o: Cortona, Etruscan Curtun, sits high on a spur of Monte Sant'Egidio overlooking the Val di Chiana and Lake Trasimeno. Greek and Roman writers credited it with legendary origins, linking it to Dardanus or to Pelasgian settlers. Archaeologically it developed into a city in the 7th and 6th centuries BCE, when its first walls were built.
cortona.r: Cortona's elite built the great 'Melone' tumuli at Sodo below the town, one with a monumental stepped altar decorated with sphinxes devouring warriors. Its bronzes include a famous hanging lamp with sixteen burners. The Tabula Cortonensis, a bronze tablet of about 200 BCE found in 1992, records a land transaction among named families and is a key source for the Etruscan language and law.
cortona.e: Livy names Cortona with Perusia and Arretium among the cities that made a thirty-year truce with Rome in 310 BCE. It gradually became a Roman ally and later a municipium, overshadowed by Arretium. The Etruscan walls still underlie the medieval town.

cornovii.t: Iron Age people of the West Midlands and Welsh borders, centred on the Wrekin, whose Roman town of Viroconium became one of the largest in Britain.
cornovii.o: The Cornovii occupied Shropshire, Cheshire and parts of Staffordshire and the Welsh borderland in the late Iron Age. Their landscape was dominated by hillforts such as the Wrekin, Titterstone Clee and the Breiddin, many of which had been occupied for centuries before the Roman period.
cornovii.r: They issued no coins and used very little pottery, so their society is known mainly from hillforts and farmsteads. Livestock farming was central, and the brine springs of Cheshire supplied salt that was traded in distinctive clay containers. No rulers are named in any source, suggesting power was held by local chiefs.
cornovii.e: The Roman army advanced into the region in the 50s, and around 55 to 60 a legionary fortress was built at Wroxeter below the Wrekin, which seems to have been abandoned. When the army left, the site became Viroconium Cornoviorum, capital of their civitas in Roman Britain and later the seat of post-Roman rulers in what became the Kingdom of Powys.

county-of-holland.t: The coastal county that grew from Frisian marshland into the richest province of the Low Countries and the core of the later Dutch Republic.
county-of-holland.o: The dynasty began with Gerulf, a Frisian lord granted lands by the Carolingians in the 880s, and Dirk I, who received the land around Egmond in 922. The counts were first known as counts of West Frisia, and the name Holland ('wood land') came into use around 1100.
county-of-holland.r: The counts drained peat bogs, built dykes and founded towns such as Haarlem, Delft, Leiden and Dordrecht. Dirk III defeated an imperial army at Vlaardingen in 1018; William II was elected King of the Romans in 1247 and began the Binnenhof at The Hague. Under Floris V the towns, fishing and cloth trade grew rapidly, and water boards became a hallmark of local government.
county-of-holland.e: Holland passed to the Avesnes counts of Hainaut in 1299, the Wittelsbachs in 1345 and the Burgundian State in 1433, amid the Hook and Cod wars. Under the Habsburg Netherlands it led the revolt against Spain, and after the Act of Abjuration of 1581 it became the dominant province of the Dutch Republic.

ceutrones.t: Alpine people of the Tarentaise who guarded the Little St Bernard pass and harassed Caesar's army in 58 BCE.
ceutrones.o: The Ceutrones held the upper Isère valley, the Tarentaise in Savoy, below the Little St Bernard pass. Caesar records that they and other mountain peoples attacked his legions as they crossed the Alps in 58 BCE.
ceutrones.r: Their power rested on control of the pass, one of the main routes between Gaul and northern Italy, and on herding and trade with the Salassi of the Aosta valley.
ceutrones.e: They were subdued in the Alpine campaigns of Augustus around 15 BCE and listed on the Tropaeum Alpium. Their town Axima (Aime) became Forum Claudii Ceutronum, capital of the small province of Alpes Graiae.

colophon.t: Ionian city famed for its cavalry and wealth, home of the poets Mimnermus and Xenophanes and keeper of the oracle of Apollo at Claros.
colophon.o: Colophon lay inland north-west of Ephesus and was founded by Ionian settlers c. 1000 BCE. It was one of the twelve cities of the Ionian League and in the 8th and 7th centuries BCE grew rich and powerful, its exiles seizing Smyrna from the Aeolians.
colophon.r: Colophon had a strong landed aristocracy whose cavalry was proverbial. The elegiac poet Mimnermus and the philosopher Xenophanes were Colophonians. The oracle of Apollo at Claros lay in its territory. Gyges of the Kingdom of Lydia captured its lower town in the 7th century BCE, and it then passed to the Achaemenid Empire and the Delian League.
colophon.e: Lysimachus forced many Colophonians to move to Ephesus c. 294 BCE. The city recovered, partly through its port of Notion, called New Colophon, and passed to Rome in 133 BCE, while Claros remained a major oracle into Roman times.
colophon.re: Greek religion; oracle of Apollo at Claros

county-of-zutphen.t: A short-lived county on the IJssel that merged with Guelders in the 12th century and gave its name to one of the duchy's four quarters.
county-of-zutphen.o: The county of Zutphen took shape in the mid-11th century around the trading town on the IJssel. Its early counts held lands granted by the German kings and the bishops of Utrecht, but details of its first rulers are scarce.
county-of-zutphen.r: Zutphen was a river-trade centre on the route between the Rhine and the Zuiderzee, and the county included rich farmland in the Achterhoek. Its counts were linked by marriage to the leading families of the region.
county-of-zutphen.e: Around 1138 the heiress Ermgard of Zutphen's marriage to Gerard of Wassenberg, count of Guelders, united Zutphen with the County of Guelders. It became one of the four quarters of the later Duchy of Guelders, and the town of Zutphen joined the Hanseatic League.

catalauni.t: Gallic people of Champagne around Châlons, whose plains gave their name to the battle against Attila in 451.
catalauni.o: The Catalauni are not named by Caesar and were probably part of the Remi in his time. They are known from later Roman sources as a separate community centred on Durocatalaunum (Châlons-en-Champagne) on the Marne.
catalauni.r: Nothing is known of their pre-Roman rulers. Their chalk plains were rich farmland on the route between Reims and Langres.
catalauni.e: Durocatalaunum became a separate civitas in the late Roman period and a bishopric. The Battle of the Catalaunian Plains in 451, where Aetius and the Visigoths halted the Hunnic Empire under Attila, is named after their land.

cretan-koinon.t: Loose federation of the quarrelsome Cretan city-states, active in the Hellenistic period until the Roman conquest of the island in 69-67 BCE.
cretan-koinon.o: Crete was divided among dozens of independent cities, chief among them Knossos and Gortyn, constantly at war. A common body of Cretans (koinon) appears in the 3rd century BCE, and around 216 BCE Philip V of Macedon was recognised as its protector (prostates), seeking influence over the island and its mercenaries.
cretan-koinon.r: The koinon had a council and a common court (koinodikion) to settle disputes between cities, and issued joint decrees and treaties. It never overrode local sovereignty, and wars such as the Lyttian War of the 220s BCE continued. Cretan archers served as mercenaries across the Mediterranean, and Cretan ports harboured pirates.
cretan-koinon.e: The league was revived and dissolved several times. Rome's war on piracy brought Marcus Antonius' failed attack in 71 BCE and then Quintus Caecilius Metellus' conquest of the island in 69-67 BCE, after which Crete became a Roman province with Gortyn as its capital.

county-of-namur.t: A compact county at the meeting of the Sambre and Meuse, built around a rock fortress that later became one of the most fought-over strongholds in Europe.
county-of-namur.o: Namur emerged in the 10th century from the old district of Lomme, when local counts built their power around the castle on the rock above the Sambre and Meuse confluence. Albert I, ruling around 981, is often treated as the first well-documented count, and his family held the county for two centuries.
county-of-namur.r: Namur was a small Walloon county of river trade, forests and ironworks, an imperial fief squeezed between Liège, Hainaut, Brabant and Luxembourg. Count Henry the Blind also held Luxembourg in the 12th century. From 1263 the Dampierre counts of Flanders ruled it, and Namur's citadel grew into a major fortress.
county-of-namur.e: The bankrupt John III sold Namur to Philip the Good in 1421, and it joined the Burgundian State, then the Habsburg Netherlands. Louis XIV took the citadel in 1692 and William III retook it in 1695. France annexed the county in 1795; it is now a Belgian province.

clusium.t: Inland Etruscan city whose king Lars Porsenna, in Roman tradition, besieged Rome after the expulsion of the Tarquins.
clusium.o: Clusium, Etruscan Clevsin, modern Chiusi, overlooked the Val di Chiana, a fertile corridor linking central Etruria with the Tiber valley. It developed from Villanovan settlements and flourished from the 7th century BCE, when its distinctive canopic urns, cinerary jars with human-headed lids, show a local elite of growing wealth.
clusium.r: Clusium's power rested on agriculture in the Chiana valley and on control of routes towards the interior. Its workshops produced cinerary urns, sculptures in local stone and fine bucchero pottery, while painted tombs such as the Tomb of the Monkey show banquets and games. Roman tradition records its king Lars Porsenna, who attacked Rome around 508 BCE and possibly took it.
clusium.e: In 391 BCE Gauls attacked Clusium, an event Roman writers linked to the Gallic sack of Rome. The city came under Roman control after the wars of the early 3rd century, traditionally around the battle of Sentinum in 295 BCE, and remained a modest Roman town; Etruscan burials continued there into the 1st century BCE.

commune-of-pistoia.t: A Tuscan city-republic with some of Italy's oldest communal statutes, where the feud of Black and White Guelphs began before spreading to Florence.
commune-of-pistoia.o: Pistoia, at the foot of the Apennines between Florence and Lucca, had consuls by 1105. Its early statutes, from the 12th century, are among the oldest surviving communal law codes in Italy.
commune-of-pistoia.r: The commune was governed by consuls, then a podestà and a captain of the people. Pistoia was known for banking and metalwork and for the silver altar of Saint James in its cathedral. Around 1300 a feud within the Cancellieri family split the Guelphs into Blacks and Whites, a quarrel exported to Florence that led to Dante's exile. Florence and Lucca besieged and took Pistoia in 1305–1306.
commune-of-pistoia.e: Castruccio Castracani of Lucca seized the city in 1325. Florence later imposed a protectorate and gradually tightened control, formally annexing Pistoia in 1401, after which it remained part of the Republic of Florence.

county-of-evreux.t: A Norman county that became the appanage of a royal branch whose members, as kings of Navarre, schemed against the Valois.
county-of-evreux.o: Around 989 Duke Richard I of Normandy created the county of Évreux for his son Robert, archbishop of Rouen. Robert's descendants held it as major Norman barons, and it later passed to the Montfort family, frequently caught up in the wars between Normandy and France.
county-of-evreux.r: Évreux was a rich farming district on the road from Paris to Rouen, with a cathedral city as its centre. Philip II obtained it from John of England by the Treaty of Le Goulet in 1200. In 1307 Philip IV gave it as an appanage to his half-brother Louis, whose son married Joan II of Navarre, founding the Évreux kings of Navarre.
county-of-evreux.e: Charles the Bad of Navarre used Évreux as a base for his intrigues against John II and Charles V, who seized most of his Norman lands. In 1404 his son Charles III of Navarre exchanged Évreux with Charles VI for the duchy of Nemours, and it returned to the Kingdom of France.

commune-of-cremona.t: A rich Po valley city-republic, usually loyal to the emperors and Milan's great rival, crowned by the Torrazzo bell tower.
commune-of-cremona.o: Cremona's citizens won rights from their bishop in the late 11th century, and consuls are recorded from 1098. Commanding a crossing of the Po, the city became a major river port and soon clashed with Milan and its ally Crema.
commune-of-cremona.r: Cremona was governed by consuls and later a podestà, with a strong guild of merchants and cloth makers. It generally sided with the emperors: it helped Frederick Barbarossa destroy Crema in 1160 and was a key base for Frederick II. The Torrazzo, one of the tallest medieval bell towers in Italy, and the cathedral date from this period. In the 13th century Ghibelline strongmen such as Buoso da Dovara and Uberto Pallavicino held power.
commune-of-cremona.e: Faction struggles between the Cavalcabò and their rivals weakened the commune, and in 1334 it submitted to Azzone Visconti, becoming part of the Lordship of Milan.

coriondi.t: People of south-east Ireland known only from Ptolemy's Geography, whose name may be related to later Irish population names.
coriondi.o: The Coriondi appear in Ptolemy's Geography of about 150, placed in the interior of south-eastern Ireland, roughly in modern Counties Kilkenny, Carlow or Wexford, near the Brigantes (Ireland) and the Usdiae. As with his other Irish peoples, his information came from earlier sailors' and traders' reports.
coriondi.r: Nothing is known of their government or way of life. Some scholars have compared their name with the Coraind, a group mentioned in early Irish texts, or with British names built on the element coria, meaning a war band or host, but no identification is certain.
coriondi.e: The Coriondi disappear from the record after Ptolemy. Their region later fell within the Kingdom of Leinster and the Kingdom of Osraige.

chersonesus-taurica.t: Democratic Greek city in south-western Crimea, colony of Heraclea Pontica, whose ruins near Sevastopol preserve a whole ancient landscape of farm plots.
chersonesus-taurica.o: Colonists from Heraclea Pontica, joined according to tradition by settlers from Delos, founded Chersonesus in 422-421 BCE on a small bay in the south-west of Crimea, perhaps on the site of an earlier trading post. Over the 4th century BCE the city took control of the Heracleian peninsula and parts of the north-west Crimean coast.
chersonesus-taurica.r: Chersonesus was a democracy whose citizens swore an oath, preserved in a 3rd-century BCE inscription, to defend the city and never betray it. Its farmland was divided into regular rectangular plots, many planted with vineyards, and wine, fish and grain were its main exports. Its patron deity was the Maiden (Parthenos).
chersonesus-taurica.e: Pressed by the Scythians of Crimea under Scilurus and Palacus, the city appealed to Mithridates VI of Pontus c. 110 BCE; his general Diophantus defended it, and it passed under Pontic and later Roman protection. As Byzantine Cherson it survived into the Middle Ages, where tradition places the baptism of Vladimir of Kiev in 988.

coriosolites.t: Armorican people of northern Brittany, best known today for huge hoards of their distinctive billon coins found in Jersey.
coriosolites.o: The Coriosolites lived in the modern Côtes-d'Armor, around the Rance estuary. Caesar names them among the Armorican peoples who submitted to Publius Crassus in 57 BCE.
coriosolites.r: They issued abundant coins of base silver with stylised heads and horses. Hoards buried around the time of the Roman conquest, above all the Grouville hoard found in Jersey in 2012 with around 70,000 coins, suggest wealth from cross-Channel trade or refugees fleeing Caesar.
coriosolites.e: After joining the Veneti and the Unelli in 56 BCE they were absorbed into Gallia Lugdunensis. Their Roman capital was Fanum Martis at Corseul, with a large temple of Mars, and the name survives in Corseul.

county-of-louvain.t: The county around Leuven and Brussels from which the Reginarid counts built the Duchy of Brabant.
county-of-louvain.o: Around 1003 Lambert I the Bearded, a member of the Reginarid family, took the title of count of Louvain. He held lands around Leuven and Brussels, which was growing on the Senne, and expanded them through war with the bishops of Liège and neighbouring lords.
county-of-louvain.r: The counts ruled a fertile, densely settled region on the trade routes between the Rhine and Flanders. Brussels and Leuven grew as market towns. Godfrey I of Louvain was named duke of Lower Lorraine in 1106, giving the family the ducal title and a claim to authority over the whole region, and they also styled themselves landgraves of Brabant.
county-of-louvain.e: Around 1183 Count Henry I began using the title duke of Brabant, and after the Diet of Schwäbisch Hall in 1190 the county became the core of the Duchy of Brabant, whose dukes ruled from Brussels and Leuven.

commune-of-bergamo.t: An Alpine-foothill city-republic in Lombardy, long torn between Guelph and Ghibelline clans before falling to Milan and then Venice.
commune-of-bergamo.o: Bergamo's bishops had held much of the city's authority, but consuls are recorded by 1098. The commune grew on wool, iron from the Bergamasque valleys and its position at the mouth of the Alpine valleys, and fought frequent border wars with Brescia.
commune-of-bergamo.r: Consuls and later a podestà governed with a large council. Bergamo joined the Lombard League in 1167 against Frederick Barbarossa, though it often leaned towards the emperors. In the 13th and 14th centuries the city was split between the Ghibelline Suardi and the Guelph Colleoni and Rivola families, whose feuds repeatedly invited outside lords into the upper town.
commune-of-bergamo.e: In 1332 Azzone Visconti took Bergamo into the Lordship of Milan. The Republic of Venice conquered it in 1428 and held it until 1797, when it briefly became the Republic of Bergamo.

celtici.t: Celtic communities of south-western Iberia, said by Pliny to have migrated from Celtiberia, living in the Alentejo and western Andalusia.
celtici.o: Strabo and Pliny describe Celtici in the south-west, between the Guadiana and the Atlantic and in the Beturia region of Extremadura and Huelva. Pliny says they came from the Celtiberians, as shown by their religion, language and town names, though the date of their arrival is uncertain, probably from the 5th century BCE.
celtici.r: They lived in fortified settlements such as Nertobriga and Mirobriga, whose -briga names are Celtic. Their society of farmers and herders lay close to the mining districts of the Sierra Morena. They seem to have been a group of communities rather than a single polity.
celtici.e: Their territory was drawn into Hispania Ulterior and was pacified after the Lusitanian wars and the campaigns of Decimus Junius Brutus from 138 BCE. Under Augustus it was split between Lusitania and Baetica.

cantiaci.t: The people of Kent, first named by Julius Caesar, whose four kings attacked his ships in 54 BCE and whose coast saw the Roman landing of 43.
cantiaci.o: Kent was the part of Britain closest to Gaul, and Caesar described its people as the most civilised of the Britons, much like the Gauls in custom. When he crossed in 55 and 54 BCE, Cantium was divided among four kings, Cingetorix, Carvilius, Taximagulus and Segovax, who attacked his beached fleet at the command of Cassivellaunus and were driven off.
cantiaci.r: Kent was densely farmed and closely tied to the Continent, receiving Gallo-Belgic coins and producing its own issues, including early cast potin coins. Oppida grew at Canterbury, Rochester and Bigbury. In the decades before the Claudian invasion, coins of Dubnovellaunus and later the influence of Cunobelinus of the Catuvellauni suggest Kent fell under the sway of more powerful northern neighbours.
cantiaci.e: The Roman army landed at Richborough in 43, and Kent was quickly absorbed into Roman Britain. Its people formed the civitas of the Cantiaci, governed from Durovernum Cantiacorum, the later Canterbury. The old name lived on in the Kingdom of Kent and the modern county.

county-of-chiny.t: A small Ardennes county on the Semois, on whose lands the Cistercian abbey of Orval was founded, before it was absorbed by Luxembourg.
county-of-chiny.o: The county emerged in the mid-10th century in the southern Ardennes, in the frontier region between the Lotharingian duchies and France. Its first known count, Otto of Warcq, built a castle at Chiny on the Semois, and his descendants extended their lands towards Ivoix and Montmédy.
county-of-chiny.r: Chiny was a wooded, thinly settled county of castles, iron working and abbeys. The counts sponsored the abbey of Orval, founded in 1070 and later Cistercian, which became the county's main religious centre. They were vassals of the Empire, connected by marriage to Bar, Namur and Loon.
county-of-chiny.e: In 1226 Countess Jeanne married Arnold of Loon, joining Chiny to the County of Loon. After the Loon line ended, the county was sold in 1364 to Wenceslaus, duke of Luxembourg, and merged into the County of Luxembourg; it lies today in Belgium.

consoranni.t: Pyrenean people of the upper Salat valley who gave their name to the Couserans district of the Ariège.
consoranni.o: Known from Pliny and later Roman sources, the Consoranni lived in the central Pyrenees in the modern Ariège, between the Convenae and the Volcae Tectosages. Little else is recorded of them before the Roman conquest.
consoranni.r: No rulers or institutions are known.
consoranni.e: Their land came under Roman control during the conquest of Aquitania. Their chief town, Lugdunum Consoranorum, later took the name of a bishop, Saint-Lizier, and the region kept the name Couserans.
