county-of-forez.t: A county of the upper Loire, ruled from Montbrison, that separated from Lyon in 1173 and passed to the dukes of Bourbon.
county-of-forez.o: In the 10th and 11th centuries a single family held the counties of Lyon and Forez, contesting control of Lyon with its archbishops. The register dates the county from around 1000. By the 1173 agreement known as the Permutatio, Count Guy II gave up his rights in Lyon to the archbishop and kept Forez.
county-of-forez.r: The counts ruled from Montbrison over a land of plains and hills on the upper Loire, founding towns and abbeys. They cultivated close ties with the French crown and with the lords of Beaujeu. The county's customs and archives are unusually well preserved, including the 15th-century Armorial of Forez.
county-of-forez.e: In 1371 the heiress Anne of Forez married Louis II, Duke of Bourbon, and the county joined the Duchy of Bourbon. After Francis I confiscated the lands of Constable Charles of Bourbon, Forez was united with the Kingdom of France in 1531.

caere.t: Coastal Etruscan city, now Cerveteri, famed for its vast tomb-city of the Banditaccia and its ports open to Greek and Phoenician traders.
caere.o: Caere, Etruscan Caisra, Greek Agylla, rose on a tufa plateau near the Tyrrhenian coast north-west of Rome. Villanovan villages united into a city during the 8th century BCE, and by the 7th century the princely Regolini-Galassi tomb shows great wealth from metals and long-distance trade.
caere.r: Caere looked to the sea through its ports, Pyrgi, Alsium and Punicum. At Pyrgi the gold tablets of about 500 BCE, written in Etruscan and Phoenician, record king Thefarie Velianas dedicating a shrine to the goddess Uni-Astarte. Caere joined Carthage against the Phocaean Greeks at Alalia around 540 BCE, kept a treasury at Delphi and produced painted Caeretan hydriae and the famous Sarcophagus of the Spouses.
caere.e: Caere was long on friendly terms with Rome, sheltering Roman sacred objects during the Gallic sack of 390 BCE and receiving a form of citizenship without the vote. After a brief revolt it lost half its territory in 273 BCE and became a Roman town. Its necropolises are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

caeroesi.t: One of the Germani Cisrhenani of the Ardennes and Eifel, who joined the Belgic coalition against Caesar in 57 BCE.
caeroesi.o: Caesar names the Caeroesi with the Condrusi, Eburones and Paemani as peoples called Germani living west of the Rhine. They are usually placed in the Eifel, between the Treveri and the Eburones.
caeroesi.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or settlements.
caeroesi.e: In 57 BCE they promised, together with the other Germani Cisrhenani, some forty thousand warriors to the Belgic league against Caesar. After the conquest they vanish from the record, their land probably absorbed by the Treveri or the Tungri.

county-of-champagne.t: The county of the great Champagne fairs, where Flemish cloth met Italian merchants and the court of Troyes nurtured Chrétien de Troyes.
county-of-champagne.o: The counties of Troyes and Meaux were built up in the 10th century by Herbert the Old of Vermandois and passed around 1022 to Odo II of Blois. A younger branch of the Blois family took Troyes, and Count Hugh was styled count of Champagne by around 1102. Theobald II reunited Blois and Champagne in the 12th century.
county-of-champagne.r: The counts protected the cycle of fairs at Troyes, Provins, Lagny and Bar-sur-Aube, which made Champagne the commercial crossroads of 12th- and 13th-century Europe. Henry the Liberal and Marie de France made Troyes a literary centre, home of Chrétien de Troyes. Count Theobald IV, a trouvère poet, became king of Navarre in 1234.
county-of-champagne.e: Countess Joan I married Philip IV in 1284, and when their son Louis X became king in 1314, Champagne passed into the royal domain of the Kingdom of France. The fairs had already declined as sea routes to Flanders opened.

ce.t: A Pictish province named in the legend of the seven sons of Cruithne, probably in Mar and Buchan in north-east Scotland.
ce.o: Ce is listed among the seven Pictish provinces, named after the sons of Cruithne. It is usually placed in Aberdeenshire, around Mar and Buchan, partly because the hill Bennachie may preserve its name.
ce.r: Nothing is known of its rulers or institutions. The area is rich in Pictish symbol stones and hillforts, such as Bennachie's Mither Tap, suggesting an organised society within the wider Pictish kingdom.
ce.e: Ce disappeared as a distinct unit when Pictland became part of the Kingdom of Scotland. The later mormaerdoms or earldoms of Mar and Buchan may continue its territory.

carnonacae.t: People of north-west Scotland named in Ptolemy's Geography, usually placed on the coast of Wester Ross.
carnonacae.o: The Carnonacae appear in Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 on the western coast of the Scottish Highlands, north of the Creones and south of the Caereni, roughly in modern Wester Ross. Their name may contain a Celtic element meaning cairn or horn, perhaps referring to rocky headlands.
carnonacae.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers or institutions. The coast of Wester Ross supported small populations living in roundhouses and duns, with brochs appearing along the Atlantic seaboard in the last centuries BCE. These tall drystone towers suggest local elites able to organise considerable labour.
carnonacae.e: The Carnonacae do not appear in any later source. Their territory later formed part of the lands of the Picts and, from the 9th century, came under strong Norse influence.

county-of-nevers.t: A Loire county in Burgundy's orbit that passed through Flemish, Burgundian and Cleves hands before becoming a duchy in 1539.
county-of-nevers.o: Around 990 Otto-William, count of Burgundy, gave the county of Nevers to his son-in-law Landry, who founded its first dynasty. Landry's descendants also held Auxerre and Tonnerre, giving the counts a large lordship along the upper Loire and the Yonne.
county-of-nevers.r: Nevers lay on the Loire between the royal domain and the Duchy of Burgundy, with forests, ironworks and river trade. Several counts went on crusade, and Count William III joined the Second Crusade. In the 13th and 14th centuries the county passed by marriage to the Flemish counts, including Louis of Nevers, and then to a younger branch of the Valois dukes of Burgundy.
county-of-nevers.e: In 1491 it passed to the house of Cleves, and in 1539 Francis I raised it to a duchy-peerage for François de Clèves. The Duchy of Nevers later went to the Gonzagas and the Mazarins, and lost its last rights in the Revolution.

callatis.t: Dorian colony of Heraclea Pontica on the Dobruja coast, a grain-trading city that defied Lysimachus and later allied with Rome, at modern Mangalia.
callatis.o: Callatis was founded by colonists from Heraclea Pontica on the western Black Sea coast, probably in the late 6th century BCE, though some sources place the foundation later. Its fertile hinterland in southern Dobruja made it a natural centre for grain exports, and it grew alongside the Milesian colonies of Histria, Tomis and Odessos.
callatis.r: Callatis kept the Doric dialect and institutions of its mother city, with cults of Apollo, Dionysus and Heracles. It traded grain, wine and craft goods with the Getae of the interior and struck its own coinage. In 313 BCE it led the Pontic cities in revolt against Lysimachus, withstanding a long siege that ended around 309 BCE.
callatis.e: In the 1st century BCE Callatis concluded a formal treaty with Rome, a rare surviving text of its kind. After the campaign of Marcus Terentius Varro Lucullus in 72-71 BCE it lay within the Roman sphere and later in the province of Moesia. The site is the modern Romanian town of Mangalia.

county-of-armagnac.t: A Gascon county whose counts gave their name to a faction in France's civil war and fought Louis XI to the bitter end.
county-of-armagnac.o: Armagnac was carved out of the duchy of Gascony around 960 for Bernard the Squinter, a younger son of the Gascon ducal house. His descendants ruled the hill country around Auch and Lectoure and gradually gathered neighbouring counties such as Fezensac and Rodez.
county-of-armagnac.r: The counts were among the greatest lords of the south-west, shifting between the English in Guyenne and the French crown. Bernard VII became constable of France and led the Armagnac party against the Burgundians in the civil war of the 1410s until his murder in Paris in 1418. The land was known for wine and its brandy, later named after it.
county-of-armagnac.e: Count John V defied Louis XI and was killed when royal troops took Lectoure in 1473. The last count, Charles I, died in 1497, and the county passed to the duke of Alençon and later to the house of Albret before returning to the Kingdom of France.

county-of-pallars-sobira.t: A remote Pyrenean county around Sort whose counts kept a degree of independence until 1491, the last of the old Catalan counties to be extinguished.
county-of-pallars-sobira.o: It was formed in 1011 when Count Sunyer of Pallars divided his lands between his sons. Guillem II received the high valleys of the Noguera Pallaresa around Sort and the Àneu valleys, while his brother Ramon III took the lower County of Pallars Jussà.
county-of-pallars-sobira.r: A mountain land of pastures, iron and small villages, Pallars Sobirà was ruled by a line of counts from Sort and the castle of Valencia d'Àneu. They became vassals of the Counts of Barcelona and later the Crown of Aragon, but kept wide local powers. Many bore the names Artau and Hug Roger.
county-of-pallars-sobira.e: Count Hug Roger III sided against King John II in the Catalan civil war of 1462-1472 and later resisted Ferdinand II. Defeated in 1487, he lost his county, which was confiscated in 1491 and given to the Cardona family as the Marquisate of Pallars.

carausian-empire.t: Breakaway Roman regime in Britain and northern Gaul, founded by the admiral Carausius in 286, the first time Britain was ruled as a separate realm.
carausian-empire.o: Carausius, a Menapian from the Low Countries, commanded the Roman fleet charged with clearing Frankish and Saxon pirates from the Channel. Accused of keeping captured plunder for himself and sentenced to death by Maximian, he declared himself emperor in 286, taking control of Britain and part of northern Gaul with his fleet.
carausian-empire.r: Carausius ruled from London and Boulogne, presenting himself as a legitimate colleague of Diocletian and Maximian. His coins, minted at London and another British mint, carried slogans such as RESTITVTOR BRITANNIAE and EXPECTATE VENI, quoting Virgil. He kept a strong fleet, repelled Maximian's attempted invasion in 289 and may have begun forts of the Saxon Shore.
carausian-empire.e: In 293 Constantius Chlorus captured Boulogne, and Carausius was murdered by his finance minister Allectus, who took power. In 296 Constantius invaded; his prefect Asclepiodotus defeated and killed Allectus, and Constantius entered London, as the Arras medallion celebrates. Britain returned to Roman Britain.

carvetii.t: People of the Eden valley in Cumbria, known almost entirely from Roman inscriptions naming their self-governing civitas at Carlisle.
carvetii.o: The Carvetii lived in the Eden valley and around Carlisle in what is now Cumbria. They are not named by any ancient historian, and they may originally have been a section of the Brigantes that the Romans recognised as a separate community after the conquest of the north in the 70s.
carvetii.r: Their existence is known from inscriptions: a milestone of 223 from near Brougham names the civitas Carvetiorum, and a tombstone from Old Penrith records a councillor of the Carvetii. These show a self-governing community with a council, administered from Luguvalium, Carlisle, close to Hadrian's Wall. The countryside was farmed by native communities living in enclosed settlements.
carvetii.e: As one of the northernmost civitates of Roman Britain, the community lasted until Roman rule ended around 410. Carlisle remained an important centre afterwards, and the area later formed part of British kingdoms such as Rheged.

county-of-comminges.t: A Pyrenean county around Saint-Bertrand-de-Comminges whose counts fought on the Occitan side in the Albigensian Crusade.
county-of-comminges.o: Counts of Comminges appear in the early 10th century, governing the upper Garonne valley around the old Roman town of Lugdunum Convenarum, later Saint-Bertrand-de-Comminges. They were related to the counts of Couserans and Carcassonne and drifted into the orbit of the counts of Toulouse.
county-of-comminges.r: Comminges was a mountainous land of pastoral farming, small towns and pilgrimage, centred on the cathedral of Saint-Bertrand. The counts later held Muret near Toulouse. Count Bernard IV joined Raymond VI of Toulouse against the crusaders and was present at the battle of Muret in 1213, where Peter II of Aragon was killed.
county-of-comminges.e: The comital line ended with Countess Marguerite, whose disputed inheritance was settled in favour of the crown; Charles VII annexed Comminges to the Kingdom of France in 1454. The name survives as a region of the Haute-Garonne.

county-palatine-of-pembroke.t: A Norman marcher lordship in south-west Wales, base of Strongbow's invasion of Ireland and birthplace of Henry VII.
county-palatine-of-pembroke.o: Arnulf de Montgomery built the first castle at Pembroke in 1093, and it held out against Welsh counter-attacks. In 1138 King Stephen made Gilbert de Clare Earl of Pembroke, giving the lordship palatine powers. English and Flemish settlers occupied south Pembrokeshire, creating the 'Little England beyond Wales'.
county-palatine-of-pembroke.r: The earls exercised royal-style jurisdiction within the county. Gilbert's son Richard de Clare, Strongbow, led the invasion of Ireland in 1170 from here. William Marshal, who married Strongbow's heiress, rebuilt Pembroke Castle with its great round keep. Later holders included the Valence and Hastings families and Jasper Tudor, whose nephew Henry VII was born in the castle in 1457.
county-palatine-of-pembroke.e: The Laws in Wales Act of 1536 ended its special status, and Pembroke became the core of Pembrokeshire. The earldom title continued in the Herbert family.

commune-of-arezzo.t: A Ghibelline city-republic of eastern Tuscany whose defeat at Campaldino in 1289 began its long decline before the power of Florence.
commune-of-arezzo.o: Arezzo, an old Etruscan and Roman town, was dominated by its powerful bishops, but consuls appear by 1098. The commune grew in the 12th century, contesting control of the town and the rural castles with the bishops and with neighbouring Siena.
commune-of-arezzo.r: Governed by consuls, then a podestà and later priors, Arezzo was generally Ghibelline. Its bishops remained political leaders: Guglielmino degli Ubertini died fighting Florence at Campaldino in 1289, and Guido Tarlati, bishop and lord from 1312 to 1327, expanded the city's territory and rebuilt its walls. The poet Petrarch was born in the city in 1304, his family having been exiled from Florence.
commune-of-arezzo.e: After Tarlati's death the city fell under outside lords and was racked by faction. In 1384 the French captain Enguerrand de Coucy sold it to the Republic of Florence, which ruled it for the rest of its history.

catana.t: Chalcidian Greek city at the foot of Mount Etna, home of the lawgiver Charondas, which was twice emptied of its people by Sicilian tyrants.
catana.o: Chalcidian colonists from Naxos founded Catana in 729 BCE, led by Euarchus, on the coast south of Mount Etna, in a fertile plain watered by the Simeto. The site had a good harbour and access to the Sicel interior.
catana.r: Catana was known for the laws of Charondas, adopted by other Chalcidian cities in Sicily and southern Italy. In 476 BCE Hieron I of Syracuse moved its people to Leontini, resettled it with Dorians and renamed it Aetna, celebrated by Pindar and Aeschylus; the original citizens returned in 461 BCE. It served as Athens' base during the Sicilian Expedition in 415 BCE. Its farmland and wine benefited from Etna's volcanic soil, though eruptions repeatedly struck it.
catana.e: In 403 BCE Dionysius I captured Catana and sold its people into slavery, settling Campanian mercenaries there. It recovered under later rulers and in 263 BCE was one of the first Sicilian cities taken by Rome, which carried off its sundial. Roman Catina became a prosperous town, today Catania.

county-of-maine.t: A county around Le Mans, long fought over by Anjou and Normandy, which became part of the Plantagenet heartland and later a royal appanage.
county-of-maine.o: Counts of Maine appear in the mid-10th century, ruling from Le Mans between the stronger principalities of Anjou, Normandy and Brittany. Count Herbert I, known as Wakedog, defended it against Fulk Nerra of Anjou in the early 11th century.
county-of-maine.r: Maine was a land of farming and forests, with a strong bishop and an assertive town: Le Mans formed one of the first urban communes in France around 1070. William the Conqueror took the county in 1063, but Count Elias of La Flèche recovered it, and his daughter's marriage to Fulk V joined it to Anjou.
county-of-maine.e: After Philip II seized it in 1204, Maine became part of the royal domain and was granted as an appanage to the Anjou princes. On the death of Charles of Maine in 1481 it returned permanently to the Kingdom of France.

county-of-provence.t: The Mediterranean county between the Rhône and the Alps that passed from Catalan to Angevin counts and was bequeathed to France in 1481.
county-of-provence.o: Under the kings of Arles, Boso of Arles held comital power in Provence around the mid-10th century. His son William the Liberator drove the Saracens from their base at Fraxinetum in 973 and became effective ruler of the region, founding the first comital dynasty.
county-of-provence.r: In 1112 the heiress Douce married Ramon Berenguer III of Barcelona, bringing Catalan counts who fostered troubadour culture and Mediterranean trade. Raymond Berengar IV's daughter Beatrice married Charles of Anjou in 1246, and the Angevin counts, also kings of Naples, ruled from Aix and Naples. The popes settled at Avignon, on the county's edge, in the 14th century.
county-of-provence.e: Queen Joanna I adopted Louis I of Anjou, whose line held Provence until 1481. That year Charles of Maine, heir of René of Anjou, bequeathed it to Louis XI, and Provence was united with the Kingdom of France, while keeping its own estates and parliament at Aix.

clazomenae.t: Ionian city on the Gulf of Smyrna, birthplace of the philosopher Anaxagoras, which moved onto an offshore islet to escape Persian attack.
clazomenae.o: Clazomenae was founded by Ionian settlers, traditionally from Colophon, on the southern shore of the Gulf of Smyrna c. 1000 BCE. It joined the Ionian League and in the 7th century BCE helped found Abdera, a first attempt later renewed by Teos, and traded at Naucratis in Egypt.
clazomenae.r: Clazomenae was known for painted terracotta sarcophagi and olive oil. After the Ionian Revolt its people moved to an islet just offshore for safety. Anaxagoras, who taught that mind orders the cosmos, was born there c. 500 BCE. It belonged to the Delian League and was fought over during the Peloponnesian War.
clazomenae.e: The King's Peace of 387 BCE named Clazomenae as Persian territory. Alexander linked the island to the mainland by a causeway. Under Hellenistic kings and then Rome, from 133 BCE in the province of Asia, it slowly declined.

carnutes.t: Gallic people of the middle Loire, whose land held the annual assembly of the druids and whose massacre at Cenabum began the revolt of 52 BCE.
carnutes.o: The Carnutes lived between the Seine and the Loire, around Autricum (Chartres) and Cenabum (Orléans). Caesar reports that their territory was considered the centre of all Gaul, where the druids met each year in a sacred place to judge disputes.
carnutes.r: They were ruled by a nobility, and Caesar installed Tasgetius as their king, but he was murdered in 54 BCE. Cenabum, on the Loire, was a busy trading town where Roman merchants lived.
carnutes.e: In early 52 BCE the Carnutes killed the Roman traders at Cenabum, the signal for the revolt of Vercingetorix. Caesar sacked the town and in 51 BCE executed their leader Gutuater. Under Rome Autricum became Chartres and Cenabum was refounded as Aurelianum, later Orléans.

cenel-loairn.t: A leading kindred of Dal Riata in northern Argyll, rivals of Cenel nGabrain, whose descendants may later have ruled Moray.
cenel-loairn.o: Cenel Loairn claimed descent from Loarn mac Eirc, said to be a brother of Fergus Mor, the legendary founder of Dal Riata. By the 7th century it controlled Lorn, Mull and neighbouring districts in northern Argyll, with its main stronghold at Dunollie near Oban.
cenel-loairn.r: Like other Dal Riatan kindreds it owed naval service and tribute recorded in the Senchus fer nAlban. Its kings competed with Cenel nGabrain for the kingship of all Dal Riata, and in the late 7th and early 8th centuries Ferchar Fota and his son Selbach held that position. Selbach burned Dunollie in 701 and later rebuilt it.
cenel-loairn.e: Selbach's defeat at sea in 719 and Pictish conquest under Oengus son of Fergus in the 730s broke Cenel Loairn's power. Later Scottish genealogies traced the rulers of the Kingdom of Moray, including Macbeth, to this kindred, though the link is debated.

county-of-hainaut.t: A cloth and coal county of the southern Low Countries, ruled from Mons for nine centuries and long linked by marriage to Flanders and Holland.
county-of-hainaut.o: Hainaut grew out of a Carolingian district on the Scheldt and Sambre. Around 898 Reginar Longneck, a leading Lotharingian noble, held comital power there, and his descendants, the Reginarids, struggled with the German kings for control. By the 11th century the county was centred on Mons and Valenciennes.
county-of-hainaut.r: Hainaut lay within the Holy Roman Empire but faced France, and its counts played both sides. The marriage of Richilde to Baldwin VI of Flanders in 1051 began a long Flemish link; Baldwin IX of Flanders, count of Hainaut, became the first Latin emperor of Constantinople in 1204. Towns grew rich on cloth, and the countryside later on coal.
county-of-hainaut.e: Hainaut was united with Holland under the Avesnes counts from 1299, and Jacqueline of Bavaria lost both to Philip the Good of the Burgundian State in 1433. The Treaty of Nijmegen of 1678 gave its south to France; the rest stayed in the Spanish Netherlands and Austrian Netherlands until French annexation in 1795.

commune-of-viterbo.t: A papal city-commune north of Rome that hosted popes in the 13th century and gave the Church the longest papal election in its history.
commune-of-viterbo.o: Viterbo grew on the Via Cassia in northern Lazio, and consuls governing the town are recorded by 1095. It expanded by subduing neighbouring towns and fought a long rivalry with the Commune of Rome, while recognising the distant overlordship of the Papal States.
commune-of-viterbo.r: The commune was ruled by consuls, then a podestà, while rival clans such as the Gatti and the prefects of Vico fought for control. From the mid-13th century popes often lived there, and the Palazzo dei Papi was built for them. The election of 1268–1271 dragged on for almost three years until the townspeople locked the cardinals in and removed the roof, leading to the conclave rules of Gregory X.
commune-of-viterbo.e: In the 14th century Giovanni di Vico made himself lord of the city until Cardinal Albornoz restored papal authority in 1354. After further strife the town came under direct papal government at the end of the century and remained part of the Papal States until 1870.

cavares.t: Gallic people of the lower Rhône whose towns became Avignon, Cavaillon and Orange.
cavares.o: Strabo names the Cavares as the leading people between the Durance and the Isère, east of the Rhône. Their towns included Avennio (Avignon), Cabellio (Cavaillon) and Arausio (Orange), and they had close commercial ties with Massalia.
cavares.r: Strabo describes them as already largely Romanised in his day. Little is known of their earlier rulers.
cavares.e: They came under Rome after 121 BCE. In 105 BCE the Cimbri and Teutones destroyed two Roman armies at Arausio in their land, one of Rome's worst defeats. Arausio was refounded as a colony for veterans of the Second Legion, with its famous theatre and arch.

corieltauvi.t: East Midlands people who issued coins under paired rulers and buried the Hallaton Treasure, and who passed under Roman rule largely without resistance.
corieltauvi.o: The Corieltauvi occupied Leicestershire, Lincolnshire, Nottinghamshire and parts of the surrounding counties in the late Iron Age; the older name Coritani was corrected after an inscription naming them was found. They grew from local farming communities on the river valleys and wolds, with major centres at Leicester, Old Sleaford and Lincoln.
corieltauvi.r: From the late 1st century BCE they issued gold and silver coins, often with two names together, such as VEP CORF or AVN COST, which may point to joint rule; later issues name Volisios and Dumnocoveros. The Hallaton Treasure, a ritual hoard of more than 5,000 coins and a Roman cavalry helmet, shows close contact with Rome before the conquest. Pottery and iron-working flourished.
corieltauvi.e: The region was occupied soon after 43, apparently with little fighting, and by 47 Roman forts and the legio IX at Lincoln held the area. The people formed the civitas of the Corieltauvi, governed from Ratae Corieltauvorum, modern Leicester, within Roman Britain.

county-of-pallars-jussa.t: The lower half of the Pyrenean county of Pallars, centred on Tremp, which passed to the Crown of Aragon in 1192.
county-of-pallars-jussa.o: When Count Sunyer of Pallars died in 1011, his lands were divided between his sons: Ramon III received the southern, lower part around Tremp and the Noguera Pallaresa valley, while his brother Guillem took the mountainous north, the County of Pallars Sobirà.
county-of-pallars-jussa.r: Pallars Jussà was a frontier county facing the Taifa of Lérida and expanded south by conquest. Its counts were often at odds with their cousins in the north and with the powerful frontier lord Arnau Mir de Tost. Like other Catalan counties, it was organised through castles, feudal oaths and monastic foundations such as Santa Maria de Gerri.
county-of-pallars-jussa.e: In 1192 Countess Dolça bequeathed the county to Alfonso II of Aragon, who incorporated it into the Crown of Aragon. Its lands later formed part of the Principality of Catalonia.
